title: TypeScript Fundamentals Part 2
excerpt: Take your TypeScript skills to the next level by learning conditions, loops, array methods, type inference, and async/await. These core concepts will help you write cleaner, more efficient, and easier-to-maintain TypeScript code.
html:
Making Decisions with if

Sometimes your program needs to make a decision.

For example, imagine your application has two types of users:

  • Admin

  • Employee

If the user is an administrator, they should see the Admin Dashboard. Otherwise, they should see the Employee Dashboard.

Create a file called if-example.ts.

const userRole = "Admin";

if (userRole === "Admin") {
  console.log("Opening Admin Dashboard...");
}

Run the program.

tsx if-example.ts

Output

Opening Admin Dashboard...

Let's understand what's happening.

The if statement checks whether a condition is true.

userRole === "Admin"

If the condition is true, the code inside the curly braces runs.

If it's false, the program simply skips it.

You'll use this pattern frequently in automation.

For example:

  • Check if a user is logged in.

  • Verify whether an element is visible.

  • Decide which environment to test.

  • Check whether a feature is enabled.

Using if...else

What if we want to handle both situations?

Let's improve the previous example.

const userRole = "Employee";

if (userRole === "Admin") {
  console.log("Opening Admin Dashboard...");
} else {
  console.log("Opening Employee Dashboard...");
}

Output

Opening Employee Dashboard...

The else block runs whenever the if condition is false.

Think of it as saying,

"If this condition isn't true, do something else."

This makes your programs much smarter.

Using else if

Sometimes there are more than two possible outcomes.

Imagine you're testing three different environments.

  • Development

  • QA

  • Production

const environment = "QA";
if (environment === "Development") {
  console.log("Running tests on the Development environment.");
} else if (environment === "QA") {
  console.log("Running tests on the QA environment.");
} else {
  console.log("Running tests on the Production environment.");
}

Output

Running tests on the QA environment.

The program checks each condition from top to bottom.

As soon as one condition matches, it stops checking the rest.

You'll often use this approach when different test environments require different configurations.

A Quick Look at switch

When you have many possible values, a switch statement can sometimes be easier to read.

Here's the same example written with switch.

const browser = "Firefox";

switch (browser) {
  case "Chromium":
    console.log("Launching Chromium...");
    break;

  case "Firefox":
    console.log("Launching Firefox...");
    break;

  case "WebKit":
    console.log("Launching WebKit...");
    break;

  default:
    console.log("Unknown browser.");
}

Output

Launching Firefox...

The break statement tells the program to stop checking other cases after finding a match.

You won't use switch as often as if, but it's good to know because you'll occasionally see it in larger projects.

Repeating Tasks with Loops

Imagine you're testing five different users.

Without a loop, you might write something like this.

console.log("Testing Sarah");
console.log("Testing John");
console.log("Testing David");
console.log("Testing Emma");
console.log("Testing Michael");

This works, but it quickly becomes repetitive.

Loops allow us to write the code once and repeat it as many times as needed.

The for Loop

The for loop is useful when you know exactly how many times something should happen.

for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= 3; attempt++) {
  console.log(`Login Attempt ${attempt}`);
}

Output

Login Attempt 1
Login Attempt 2
Login Attempt 3

Let's understand the loop.

let attempt = 1

Starts the counter at 1.

attempt <= 3

Keeps the loop running while the value is less than or equal to 3.

attempt++

Increases the value by one after every iteration.

This type of loop is useful when you know exactly how many times something should happen.

For example:

  • Retry a failed operation three times.

  • Repeat a test multiple times.

  • Generate sample test data.

The for...of Loop

This is the loop you'll probably use most often in Playwright.

Imagine we want to test several browsers.

const browsers = [
  "Chromium",
  "Firefox",
  "WebKit"
];

for (const browser of browsers) {
  console.log(`Running tests on ${browser}`);
}

Output

Running tests on Chromium
Running tests on Firefox
Running tests on WebKit

The loop automatically goes through every item in the array.

You don't have to worry about indexes or counters.

That's why many automation engineers prefer for...of when working with arrays.

Some common Playwright examples include:

  • Testing multiple users.

  • Checking every product in a list.

  • Validating table rows.

  • Verifying menu items.

Whenever you're working with an array, for...of is usually a great choice.

The while Loop

A while loop repeats until a condition becomes false.

let failedAttempts = 1;

while (failedAttempts <= 3) {
  console.log(`Retry ${failedAttempts}`);

  failedAttempts++;
}

Output

Retry 1
Retry 2
Retry 3

Unlike the for loop, a while loop doesn't know in advance how many times it will run.

It simply asks,

"Is this condition still true?"

If the answer is yes, it keeps running.

You'll use while less often than for...of, but it's still useful in some situations.

Working with Arrays More Efficiently

Earlier we learned how arrays store multiple values.

TypeScript also gives us several built-in methods that make working with arrays much easier.

These methods are used frequently in modern JavaScript and TypeScript projects.

Let's look at the most useful ones.

forEach()

The forEach() method performs an action for every item in an array.

const browsers = [
  "Chromium",
  "Firefox",
  "WebKit"
];

browsers.forEach((browser) => {
  console.log(`Running tests on ${browser}`);
});

Output

Running tests on Chromium
Running tests on Firefox
Running tests on WebKit

This produces the same result as for...of.

Both are perfectly fine.

As you read more Playwright code, you'll see developers using both styles.

map()

The map() method creates a new array by transforming each item.

Imagine we want to display every browser name in uppercase.

const browsers = [
  "Chromium",
  "Firefox",
  "WebKit"
];

const upperCaseBrowsers = browsers.map((browser) => {
  return browser.toUpperCase();
});

console.log(upperCaseBrowsers);

Output

[ 'CHROMIUM', 'FIREFOX', 'WEBKIT' ]

The original array stays exactly the same.

map() simply creates a new one.

filter()

The filter() method keeps only the items that match a condition.

Imagine our application only supports Chromium.

const browsers = [
  "Chromium",
  "Firefox",
  "WebKit"
];

const supportedBrowsers = browsers.filter((browser) => {
  return browser === "Chromium";
});

console.log(supportedBrowsers);

Output

[ 'Chromium' ]

In automation, filter() is useful when you only want certain data instead of everything.

find()

Sometimes you only need one matching item.

That's where find() helps.

const browsers = [
  "Chromium",
  "Firefox",
  "WebKit"
];

const browser = browsers.find((browser) => {
  return browser === "Firefox";
});

console.log(browser);

Output

Firefox

Unlike filter(), which returns an array, find() returns the first matching item.

You'll often use this when searching for a specific object, user, or product in a collection.

Which One Should You Use?

You don't need to memorize every method today.

A simple guideline is enough.

Use this

When you want to...

for...of

Loop through every item

forEach()

Perform an action for every item

map()

Create a new array

filter()

Keep only matching items

find()

Find the first matching item

Type Inference

Throughout this series, we've explicitly written types like this:

const browser: string = "Chromium";
const retries: number = 3;

This is perfectly valid, but TypeScript is smart enough to figure out many types on its own.

const browser = "Chromium";
const retries = 3;
const headless = true;

Even though we didn't specify the types, TypeScript automatically understands that:

  • browser is a string

  • retries is a number

  • headless is a boolean

This is called Type Inference.

In real projects, you'll often see developers rely on type inference because it keeps the code cleaner.

So when should you write types explicitly?

A simple rule is:

  • Let TypeScript infer simple variables.

  • Add explicit types to function parameters, interfaces, and more complex objects where they improve readability.

As you gain experience, you'll naturally know when an explicit type makes your code easier to understand.

Understanding Async and Await

This is one of the most important concepts you'll encounter in Playwright. Imagine you're downloading a large file. The download takes a few seconds. While it's downloading, you don't want the rest of your program to assume the file is already available. The program needs to wait.

The same thing happens in browser automation. Opening a webpage...
Clicking a button...
Uploading a file...
Waiting for search results...
None of these actions happen instantly. They all take time.

That's why Playwright uses async and await.

Let's understand the syntax with a simple example.

async function sayHello() {
  return "Hello, World!";
}

async function greet() {
  const message = await sayHello();

  console.log(message);
}

greet();

Output

Hello, World!

Let's break it down.

The async keyword tells TypeScript that the function performs asynchronous work. The await keyword pauses the current function until the asynchronous task is complete.

Only then does the program move to the next line.

Think of await as saying:

"I'll wait here until you're finished."

This keeps your code predictable and much easier to read than older approaches.

Why Does Playwright Use Await Everywhere?

Here's a simple Playwright example.

await page.goto("https://example.com");
await page.fill("#email", "john@example.com");
await page.click("button");

Each step waits for the previous one to finish.

First the page opens. Then the email field is filled. Finally, the button is clicked.

Without await, the program could try to click the button before the page has even finished loading.

That's why you'll see await on almost every Playwright action.

Don't worry if it feels unfamiliar today. After writing a few tests, using await will become second nature.

Mini Practice Project

Let's bring together some of the concepts you've learned.

Create a file named browser-checker.ts.

interface Browser {
  name: string;
  supported: boolean;
}

const browsers: Browser[] = [
  { name: "Chromium", supported: true },
  { name: "Firefox", supported: true },
  { name: "WebKit", supported: true },
  { name: "Internet Explorer", supported: false }
];

for (const browser of browsers) {
  if (browser.supported) {
    console.log(`${browser.name} is supported.`);
  } else {
    console.log(`${browser.name} is not supported.`);
  }
}

Output

Chromium is supported.
Firefox is supported.
WebKit is supported.
Internet Explorer is not supported.

Although it's a small program, it combines several important concepts:

  • Interface

  • Array

  • Object

  • Loop

  • Condition

  • Template literal

These same building blocks appear in real automation frameworks.

Practice Exercises

Before moving on to Playwright, try completing these exercises without looking back at the examples.

Exercise 1

Create an array of five test users and print each user's name.

Exercise 2

Create an interface called Product.

Include:

  • Product name

  • Price

  • In stock

Create three products and print their information.

Exercise 3

Create a program that checks whether a browser is supported.

If it is, print:

Otherwise, print:
